raw_text:
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were developed to address a central limitation of permanent metallic drug-eluting stents (DES): the vessel remains caged after the period when mechanical support and drug delivery are needed. The conceptual advantages were compelling—late restoration of vasomotion, adaptive remodeling, easier future bypass grafting or reintervention, and potentially less very-late thrombosis once the scaffold disappeared. The field began with the self-expanding poly-L-lactic acid Igaki-Tamai stent, which demonstrated human feasibility and surprisingly durable long-term outcomes, albeit without modern antiproliferative drug elution [1], [2]. Subsequent reviews framed BVS as a “fourth revolution” in percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), but also emphasized that clinical benefit would depend on achieving metallic-stent-like deliverability, radial strength, strut thickness, and healing [3].

The first widely adopted coronary BVS was the Absorb everolimus-eluting scaffold, a poly-L-lactic acid platform with poly-D,L-lactide everolimus coating. Early first-in-human and cohort studies showed acceptable procedural success, late lumen enlargement, return of vasomotion, and favorable intravascular imaging findings, generating substantial enthusiasm [4], [5], [6], [7]. In parallel, magnesium-based absorbable metallic scaffolds were pursued to improve acute mechanical performance. The DREAMS and later BIOSOLVE-II programs showed encouraging safety and angiographic results for drug-eluting absorbable magnesium scaffolds, supporting the broader principle that resorbable platforms were technically feasible [8], [9].

Randomized evidence, however, changed the clinical trajectory. In ABSORB III, the Absorb scaffold was noninferior to the cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stent for target-lesion failure at 1 year, but numerically more scaffold thrombosis was observed [10]. ABSORB II raised concern by failing to show superior vasomotion and by demonstrating excess target-vessel myocardial infarction and scaffold thrombosis at 3 years [11], [12]. ABSORB China provided more favorable early angiographic and clinical results, illustrating that lesion selection and implantation practice mattered, but it did not eliminate safety concerns [13]. The AIDA all-comers trial was pivotal: routine BVS use was associated with a markedly higher risk of device thrombosis than metallic DES [14]. ABSORB IV, which mandated more careful sizing and implantation technique, improved outcomes but still did not establish superiority over contemporary metallic everolimus-eluting stents [15]. In ST-elevation myocardial infarction, TROFI II showed acceptable arterial healing by optical coherence tomography, but acute thrombotic settings remained a biologically challenging niche [16].

Registry experience paralleled the trials. The GHOST-EU registry reported reasonable overall event rates but highlighted early and late scaffold thrombosis in real-world use [17]. Meta-analyses consistently found higher definite or probable device thrombosis and, in several analyses, higher target-lesion failure with Absorb compared with metallic everolimus-eluting stents [18], [19], [20], [21]. Individual-patient pooled analyses clarified the time course: excess risk was concentrated before complete bioresorption, particularly during the first 3 years, with less signal after expected scaffold degradation [22].

The causes were multifactorial. Absorb had thick struts, limited overexpansion tolerance, slower endothelialization in disturbed-flow regions, and greater susceptibility to malapposition, underexpansion, and fracture. Thrombosis studies identified small vessels, inadequate lesion preparation, underdeployment, discontinuation of dual antiplatelet therapy, and complex lesions as recurring risk factors [23]. Intracoronary imaging and pathology implicated late scaffold discontinuity, dismantling, malapposition, neoatherosclerosis, and uncovered struts in very-late events [24], [25]. Preclinical work confirmed that polymeric scaffold resorption is a prolonged biological process rather than a benign disappearance [26].

These lessons transformed BVS practice. The “PSP” implantation strategy—aggressive lesion preparation, accurate vessel sizing, and high-pressure post-dilatation—became essential rather than optional [27], [28]. Nevertheless, even optimized technique could not fully overcome first-generation device limitations, and Absorb was withdrawn from commercial availability. Contemporary revascularization guidance therefore favors new-generation metallic DES for routine PCI, while prolonged antiplatelet therapy may be considered after scaffold implantation when bleeding risk permits [29], [30].

The BVS concept remains scientifically attractive, but first-generation polymeric scaffolds demonstrated that disappearance alone is insufficient. Future devices must combine thinner struts, greater radial strength, predictable degradation, broader expansion limits, and robust deliverability with randomized evidence against best-in-class DES. Until such data emerge, BVS should be regarded as an instructive but cautionary chapter in PCI innovation rather than a routine alternative to metallic DES.
